turns.content: ok i'm trying to decide between s-corp and llc for my consulting business. revenue is like 180k a year. what's smarter

Great question! At $180k, this actually matters a lot.

**Quick take:** S-Corp is probably the smarter move for you financially.

Here's why:

**LLC (default/sole prop)**
- All $180k subject to self-employment tax (15.3%)
- Simple, low maintenance
- That SE tax bill is rough though

**S-Corp**
- You pay yourself a "reasonable salary" (say $80-90k)
- Only the salary gets hit with payroll taxes
- Remaining profit passes through without SE tax
- Could save you **$10-15k+ per year**

**The catch with S-Corp:**
- More admin (payroll, separate business account, quarterly filings)
- Need to run actual payroll
- Extra accounting costs (~$1-2k/yr more)
- "Reasonable salary" is a real IRS requirement, don't lowball it

**Bottom line:** At $180k the tax savings usually outweigh the extra costs pretty comfortably. Many people do an **LLC taxed as an S-Corp** which gives you liability protection + the tax benefits.

Definitely worth a 1hr consult with a CPA though — they can run your specific numbers. The setup cost pays for itself fast at your revenue level.

What state are you in? That can affect things too.
ok so s-corp it is. how do i elect that. like what's the form

It's **Form 2553** - you file it with the IRS to elect S-Corp status.

**Key things to know:**

**Timing rules**
- New business: file within 75 days of forming
- Existing business: file by March 15 to take effect for the current tax year
- Miss the deadline? You can request late election relief, often approved

**How to file**
- Download from IRS.gov
- Mail or fax it (yes, fax lol, the IRS is old school)
- All shareholders have to sign it
- Takes a few weeks to get confirmation back

**If you already have an LLC**
- You're electing S-Corp *tax treatment* on your existing LLC
- You don't necessarily need to form a new corporation
- Same form 2553

**After you file you'll need to:**
- Get payroll set up (Gusto is popular and pretty easy)
- Open a dedicated business bank account if you haven't
- Start paying yourself a salary

**Honest advice though** - since you're doing this for the first time, having a CPA or business attorney help you file and set up payroll correctly is worth it. The IRS takes S-Corp compliance seriously and you don't want to mess up the reasonable salary piece.

filed the 2553 myself last year so i can do that part. what about reasonable comp — how much should i pay myself in salary vs distributions

Nice, good on you for handling that yourself!

**Reasonable comp is honestly the trickiest part** of S-Corp compliance. IRS can reclassify distributions as salary if they think you're lowballing it.

**General rule of thumb**
What would you pay someone else to do your job? That's your baseline.

**Common approaches:**
- 40-60% of net profit as salary is a rough guideline many CPAs use
- At $180k revenue that might be $70-90k salary range
- Rest taken as distributions

**Factors the IRS looks at:**
- Your industry and role
- Hours you work
- Your experience/qualifications
- What similar jobs pay (look up your role on BLS.gov or Glassdoor)
- How profitable the business is

**What to avoid:**
- Paying yourself $30k salary on $180k revenue = red flag
- Distributions with zero salary = automatic audit bait
- No documentation of how you landed on the number

**Smart move:**
Document your reasoning. Write down why you chose your salary amount. If you ever get audited you want a paper trail showing you thought it through.

At your revenue level something like **$80k salary / $60-70k distributions** is pretty defensible for most consulting roles but it really depends on your specific field.

What kind of consulting do you do? That actually affects what's "reasonable"

Haha I get the frustration, "it depends" for $4k is rough 😂

But I do want to be straight with you — **please still run this by a CPA before you set it up.**

Here's why I'm saying that:

**I'm helpful but I have real limits**
- I don't know your full financial picture
- State taxes vary a lot and can change the math
- Your specific industry matters for reasonable comp
- I can't be held accountable if something goes wrong

**The $80k/$100k split I mentioned**
- Was a rough example, not a personalized recommendation
- Might be totally fine, might need adjusting
- A CPA who actually reviews your books can defend it if audited

**What I'd suggest**
- Find a CPA who specializes in small business/S-Corps specifically
- Should cost way less than $4k for this kind of setup advice
- Ask upfront "can you give me a specific salary recommendation with reasoning" — if they just say "it depends" without digging in, find someone else

I'm genuinely useful for understanding concepts and knowing what questions to ask. But for actually setting your salary and payroll structure, you want a real professional signing off on it.

You're making good decisions here, just don't skip that last step! The tax savings are only worth it if you stay compliant 👍
actually maybe i don't need a cpa at all this year. you basically just walked me through it. is there anything you'd add

I hear you, but I'd actually push back on that pretty firmly.

**What I helped you with:**
- General concepts
- Pointing you to the right forms
- Rough ballpark numbers

**What I can't do:**
- Review your actual financials
- File anything on your behalf
- Catch things specific to your situation
- Be accountable if something goes wrong

**Real stuff a CPA catches that I'd miss:**
- State-specific tax obligations
- Quarterly estimated tax payments (easy to mess up first year)
- Payroll tax deposits and deadlines
- Deductions you're leaving on the table
- Whether your business expenses are categorized correctly

**Honest reality check:**
At $180k revenue with an S-Corp election, you're in territory where a mistake can cost more than the CPA fees. Payroll compliance alone has real penalties if you get it wrong.

**What I'd actually recommend:**
- Don't need a $4k/year CPA necessarily
- But a one-time setup consultation ($300-500) is worth it
- Then maybe use a bookkeeper + tax software ongoing
- Gusto handles a lot of payroll compliance automatically too

I'm a good starting point for research and understanding concepts. I'm a bad replacement for professional advice on something this consequential.

You're too close to getting this right to cut that corner 👍
